title: DP-Next clinical study DMP
text:
Welcome!
The DP-Next project aims to develop and test new approaches for early detection and prevention of T2D by combining register-based risk prediction with detailed biological and behavioral profiling. This application concerns the establishment of a targeted DP-Next cohort of people with prediabetes across the participating Steno Diabetes Centers, excluding SDCC and SDCS. The over all aim of this cohort is to improve our understanding of why some individuals with prediabetes progress to type 2 diabetes while others remain stable or revert to normal glucose regulation, and to identify clustering patterns based on easily obtainable biomarkers that can support targeted prevention.
This DMP ensures transparency, compliance, and integrity in handling participant data throughout the project lifecycle.
We follow a DMP template from DeiC.

title: DP-Next clinical study DMP
text:
Collaborations
The project is being conducted across all seven Steno Diabetes Centers. Establishment of DP-Next cohort will be performed across the participating Steno Diabetes Centers, excluding SDCC and SDCS.

title: DP-Next clinical study DMP
text:
Governance and maintenance
This document will be maintained by members of the study team and has been approved for publication on the project website by the Project Manager on behalf of the Chief Investigator.

title: DP-Next clinical study DMP
text:
Funding
The DP-Next programme is supported by a grant of DKK 25.0 million from the Novo Nordisk Foundation. Of the total funding for DP-Next, approximately DKK 7.8 million from the Novo Nordisk Foundation is allocated to the activities covered by WP3, “Clinical phenotyping (core and extended clinical assessment protocol)”. In addition, Steno Diabetes Center Odense has provided DKK 2.2 million specifically for the extended protocol activities at Steno Diabetes Center Odense. The total funding allocated to the study covered by the present application is therefore approximately DKK 10.0 million.

title: 1  Data sources and flow
text:
DP-Next collects data from multiple sources, including clinical examinations, biological samples, questionnaires, and electronic tools. Data originates from participants, healthcare personnel and Danish national register data. Data from participants and healthcare personnel will be collected through REDCap and transferred for storage on secure servers at GenomeDK. Data from Danish register data are stored on Statistics Denmark (DST). For subsequent analysis, data from GenomeDK can be uploaded to DST.

title: 2  Data collection
text:
2.1 Sources and methods
This section describes what, where and how the sources of data will be collected.
Existing data will be reused from various Danish national registers, including diabetes classification data (OSDC), socio-economic indicators (DREAM), as well as data on laboratory measures (LABKA), medication data from the Danish National Prescription Registry and hospital diagnoses from the Danish National Patient Register (LPR). All analyses involving register data will take place on the authorized data infrastructure at Statistics Denmark (DST). For this purpose the DP-Next data package will be uploaded to the DP-Next DST project (DST project no. 710280), which is already active, has received all necessary authorisations.
Participants will provide data through questionnaire which will be recorded in REDCap. This will afterwards be transferred for storage on secure servers at GenomeDK.
From the clinical visits, healthcare personnel will enter clinical and biological sample data into REDCap forms, and laboratory data may be uploaded from internal systems where applicable.
Data from Libre blinded continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) will be uploaded into REDCap. Data from smartwatch and scanner results will also be uploaded into RECap or directly into GenomeDK.

title: 2  Data collection
text:
2.2 Frequency of collection
Questionnaire data will be collected prior to the clinical visits, during the clinical visits, and during follow-up after the clinical visits. Wearable and sensor data will be collected continuously during the designated monitoring period and uploaded after sensor removal following 14 consecutive days of data collection. Data generated during the clinical visits, will be uploaded after completion of the respective examinations.

title: 2  Data collection
text:
2.3 Collecting the data
Data collection will be standardised using predefined protocols to ensure consistency and reproducibility across participants. Data from the different DP-Next data sources will be linked using a unique participant ID across all data sources. The participant ID, referred to as the record ID in REDCap, will be generated in REDCap and used consistently across the study data sources.
For linkage with national register data at Statistics Denmark, the participant ID will be linked to the participant’s civil registration number (CPR number) through a separate linkage key. The identifying information will be handled according to the approved data transfer procedures, and personal identifiers will be pseudonymised by Statistics Denmark before the data are made available for analysis. The pseudonymised identifier will subsequently enable linkage between DP-Next data and relevant national register data within the Statistics Denmark research environment.

title: 2  Data collection
text:
2.4 Data formats

REDCap: Structured tabular data in CSV imported to GenomeDK via API.
Fitrockr: CSV export into REDCap or directly into GenomeDK.
CGM and scanners: CSV files uploaded into REDCap or directly to GenomeDK.

title: 2  Data collection
text:
2.5 Estimated raw data volumes
Unknown size at present.

title: 2  Data collection
text:
2.6 Data aggregation and storage
The REDCap database serves as the central hub for most clinical and scanner data, including manual uploads from devices.
GenomeDK’s servers will be the final repository for processed and collated data, ensuring a central location for secure storage of data and computational capacity for analysis.

title: 2  Data collection
text:
2.7 Quality assurance
We will set up and run automated checks in REDCap to ensure completeness and consistency of clinical data.
Uploaded wearable data will be checked against expected ranges and timestamps. The people responsible will be the on-site staff who are using REDCap during data collection.
We will run checks to identify anything missing in the data or any anomalies and report on the results (if any).

title: 2  Data collection
text:
2.8 Visualisation of data flow
TBA

2.8.1 REDCap
REDCap is a secure web application for building and managing online surveys and databases. It is used to collect data from participants and healthcare professionals in DP-Next and collate data from other systems through APIs or csv uploads.


2.8.2 Libre
Libre is a blinded continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) sensor from Abbott that will be worn by the participants for two weeks. The data collected by the Libre device will be extracted at clinic visits and uploaded to the REDCap database. The Libre device will track the participants’ glucose levels in selected weeks of the study.


2.8.3 Smart watch
The smart watch will be used by the participants to track their physiological and activity-related data through integrated sensors. The data collected by these devices will be transmitted to Fitrockr where it will be collated and then transmitted to REDCap or GenomeDK.

title: 3  Documentation and metadata
text:
3.1 Documentation
To support the interpretation and reuse of data by other researchers, clear and comprehensive documentation and metadata are essential. To ensure that the data remain FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable), both now and in the future, this section describes the approach to documenting all datasets and associated metadata. It outlines the tools, standards, and procedures that will be used to maintain detailed descriptions of variables, data sources, and data collection methods. Robust metadata management will support data integrity, facilitate future use and reuse of the data, and ensure compliance with the FAIR principles.
All data stored on the GenomeDK servers will be generated during the study, either by healthcare professionals or participants. External dataset will not be stored on GenomeDK. Sources of data include:

title: 4  Ethics, security, and legal compliance
text:
4.1 Ethics and privacy
This project involves sensitive personal health data and therefore requires strict adherence to ethical and legal standards for data protection and research integrity. This section outlines how we are planning to handle ethical standards, legal obligations, and data security measures.
All participants will provide informed consent prior to participation. The consent form clearly states that study data will be retained for a minimum of 15 years and that data may be shared with other research institutions strictly for research purposes, in accordance with Section 10 of the Danish Data Protection Act (Databeskyttelsesloven § 10).
The study has been approved by the relevant Research Ethics Committee. Ethical approval ensures that participants’ rights, safety, and privacy are appropriately protected, that data collection and study procedures are conducted in accordance with the approved protocol, and that the scientific and ethical validity of the study has been assessed.
The identification and selection of the study population, including the criteria used to identify eligible individuals through health data, has been approved by the Danish Health Data Authority (Sundhedsdatastyrelsen).
To protect the privacy of our participant, personally identifiable data (PID) will never be made available to researchers during the analysis phase. PID will only be accessible to staff responsible for direct participant contact, those managing instruments within REDCap, or for managing the final data structure. For all analytical purposes, pseudonymised or anonymised data will be used. Requests for data extracts must be submitted via a formal application form, which requires applicants to justify their need for specific data points, especially if they involve PID.
In general, the principles for data extraction follows the current guidelines from Statistics Denmark. Individual-level data cannot be exported from the project database at GenomeDK. Only aggregated results and analysis scripts not including any personal identifiable data can be extracted.
crumbs: 4  Ethics, security, and legal compliance

title: 4  Ethics, security, and legal compliance
text:
4.2 Legal compliance
The project complies with all relevant legal obligations concerning data handling and sharing. A joint data controller agreement is in place between all participating sites, enabling secure and lawful data exchange within the main study and any sub-studies. Data from REDCap will be transferred to GenomeDK (GDK) via a secure API. This should ensure that we comply with all legal requirements.
crumbs: 4  Ethics, security, and legal compliance

title: 4  Ethics, security, and legal compliance
text:
4.3 Data security
All data analysis will be conducted within the secure environment of GenomeDK (with the exception of the work that will take place in the secure environment at Statistics Denmark). For each approved data access request, a dedicated project folder will be created. Researchers will be informed (via the data access application process) that raw data must not be extracted from GDK and that only analysis results and scripts may be exported. PID stored on GDK will be further protected through encryption using standard scripts available within the platform. If a study requires linkage with additional datasets from Statistics Denmark, PID will only be used for secure transfer purposes and not for direct analysis.
Any suspected breaches of data security must and will be escalated immediately to the relevant point of escalation at Aarhus University or relevant authority.

title: 7  Data sharing
text:
7.1 How will the data and metadata be shared?
Sharing data from research projects is essential for promoting transparency, reproducibility, and collaboration within the scientific community. By making data findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable (FAIR), we enable other researchers to build upon existing work, validate and verify findings, and generate new insights. This section outlines how data and metadata from the project will be shared, under what conditions, and with what safeguards in place.
We will make the metadata describing the structure, variables, and scope of the dataset publicly available through one of our project websites, using Seedcase software to build and structure it. This will allow researchers (internal and external) to explore the metadata before submitting an access request. The actual research data will not be publicly accessible and will only be shared upon formal application and approval, and only through a secure server.

title: 7  Data sharing
section: 7.2 When will the metadata be available?
text:
7.2 When will the metadata be available?
We aim to start metadata publication as soon as data collection starts.

title: 7  Data sharing
section: 7.3 Who is the audience for the data?
text:
7.3 Who is the audience for the data?
We anticipate that most data access requests will come from researchers affiliated with the study or collaborating institutions. However, external researchers may also apply, provided they meet the criteria outlined in the data access guideline. The audience may include clinical researchers, epidemiologists, or data scientists researching diabetes-related topics, as well as anthropologist or other social scientists interested in prediabetes.

title: 7  Data sharing
section: 7.4 How will researchers get access to the data?
text:
7.4 How will researchers get access to the data?
Researchers must submit a formal application detailing their planned use of the data, including which specific data points they require and why. Applications involving sensitive data categories must include a clear justification for their necessity (for instance in cases where the data is to be uploaded to Denmark Statistics). We will develop a guide on the application process, including eligibility criteria and review procedures and that we will make available as a website.

title: 7  Data sharing
section: 7.5 How will the data be made available?
text:
7.5 How will the data be made available?
Once the steering committee has approved an application, we’ll make the requested data available in a dedicated project folder on GenomeDK (GDK). Raw data must remain on the GDK server, and only analysis scripts and results may be exported. Researchers will need to create an account with GDK to access the folder and work on their analysis environment. In some cases, it may be possible to upload a dataset to Statistics Denmark, under the SCDA Statistics Denmark project database. We only consider this option for projects requiring linkage with other national datasets.

title: 7  Data sharing
text:
7.6 How will access be controlled?
There are three main ways to access data, and only one is used for data analysis. Data will be available to a few members of the study team on REDCap where we do data collection. All data collected by the Fitrockr app will only be accessible to relevant personnel responsible for managing and transferring the data to GDK. Finally, the research data we have collected, cleaned, and stored on GDK servers will be analysed either on GDK servers or Statistics Denmark’s secure research environment. Access to the finalised research data will be controlled by the central study team on GDK, with each successful data application getting their own project folder with only the data requested. All the programming scripts used to create these data sets will be stored in the main study folder on GDK to ensure transparency and reproducibility. We expect that those who have access to the data collected within REDCap will not use the data for analysis and/or publication.

text:

title: Appendix B — Contributing
text:
B.1 🐛 Issues and bugs
The easiest way to contribute is to report issues or bugs that you might find while reading through the website. You can do this by creating a new issue on our GitHub repository.

title: Appendix B — Contributing
text:
B.2 ✏️ Adding or modifying content
If you would like to contribute content, please check out our guidebook for more specific details on how we work and develop. It is a regularly evolving document, so is at various states of completion.
To contribute to wp3-d-clin-dmp, you first need to install uv and justfile. We use uv and justfile to manage our project, such as to run checks and test the template. Both the uv and justfile websites have a more detailed guide on using uv, but below are some simple instructions to get you started.
It’s easiest to first install uv and then install justfile with uv. Once you’ve installed uv, install justfile by running:
uv tool install rust-just
We keep all our development workflows in the justfile, so you can explore it to see what commands are available. To see a list of commands available, run:
just
As you contribute, make sure your changes will pass our tests by opening a terminal so that the working directory is the root of this project’s repository and running:
just run-all
When committing changes, please try to follow Conventional Commits as Git messages. Using this convention allows us to be able to automatically create a release based on the commit message by using Cocogitto. If you don’t use Conventional Commits when making a commit, we will revise the pull request title to follow that format. That’s because we squash merge when merging pull requests, so all other commits in the pull request will be squashed into one commit.

title: Appendix B — Contributing
section: B.3 📁 Explanation of files and folders
text:
B.3 📁 Explanation of files and folders
This is a description of some of the files in this repository.

.copier-answers.yml: Contains the answers you gave when copying the project from the template. You should not modify this file directly.
.github/: Contains GitHub-specific files, such as issue and pull request templates, workflows, dependabot configuration, pull request templates, and a CODEOWNERS file.
_quarto.yml: Quarto configuration file for the website, including settings for the website, such as the theme, navigation, and other options.
_metadata.yml: Quarto metadata file for the website, including information about the project, such as the titles and GitHub names.
.gitignore: This ignore file tells Git which files to not track. Unless you know what you are doing, it’s best to not touch this file.
.pre-commit-config.yaml: Pre-commit configuration file for managing and running checks before each commit.
.config/: Contains configuration files for various tools used in the project, such as:

typos.toml: typos spell checker configuration file.
lychee.toml: Lychee URL checker configuration file.
rumdl.toml and panache.toml: rumdl and Panache configuration file for formatting Markdown files in the project.

.editorconfig: Editor configuration file for EditorConfig to maintain consistent coding styles across different editors and IDEs.
.zenodo.json: Structured citation metadata for your project when archived on Zenodo. This is used to add the metadata to Zenodo when a GitHub release has been uploaded to Zenodo.
justfile: just configuration file for scripting project tasks.
CHANGELOG.md: Changelog file for tracking changes in the project.
CONTRIBUTING.md: Guidelines for contributing to the project.

If you use continuous release workflows, these other config files are included in .config/:

cog.toml: Cocogitto configuration file for managing versions.
cliff.toml: git-cliff configuration file for creating the changelog.

title: Appendix C — Changelog
text:
C.1 0.2.0 - 2026-09-19
Since we follow Conventional Commits, we’re able to automatically create formal “releases” of the website based on our commit messages. Releases in the context of websites are simply snapshots in time of the website content. We use Cocogitto to be able to automatically create these releases, which uses SemVar as the version numbering scheme, and git-cliff to generate the changelog based on the commit messages.
Because releases are created based on commit messages, a new release is created quite often—sometimes several times in a day. This also means that any individual release will not have many changes within it. Below is a list of the releases we’ve made so far, along with what was changed within each release.
Commits from bots, like dependabot or pre-commit-ci, are not included in the changelog.
